title: Latency, bandwidth, throughput: the three everyone confuses
story:
Three different quantities get called speed, and a system can be excellent at one while being unusable because of another. Latency is the delay before the first result. Bandwidth is the width of the pipe. Throughput is completed work per unit time. A satellite link has enormous bandwidth and terrible latency; a system with high throughput can still feel slow to every individual user, because throughput is measured over the population and latency is experienced by a person.

The reason to keep them separate is not pedantry, it is that they do not improve at the same rate and one of them is bounded by physics. Patterson documented a consistent theme across many technologies over many years: bandwidth improves much more quickly than latency for four different technologies — disks, networks, memories and processors — and proposed as a rule of thumb that bandwidth improves by more than the square of the improvement in latency.

The magnitudes are worth holding onto. Over roughly twenty to twenty-five years across those four technologies, bandwidth improved by factors between 120 and 2200 while latency improved only by factors between 4 and 20. For disks specifically, comparing 1983 with 2003, bandwidth went from 0.6 to 86 megabytes per second while latency went from 48.3 to 5.7 milliseconds.

His explanations are structural rather than incidental, which is what makes this a design constraint rather than a temporary state. The transistor improvements that help bandwidth do not help latency the same way. Distance limits latency because the speed of light is fixed. And bandwidth is easier to sell. He quotes David Clark: bandwidth problems can be cured with money, latency problems are harder because the speed of light is fixed — you cannot bribe God.

What follows is a design instinct that recurs throughout this track. Spend bandwidth to avoid latency, never the reverse. Read ahead, prefetch, batch, send more than you were asked for, replicate data closer to where it is needed. Every one of those trades the cheap resource for the expensive one. And when somebody proposes making a system faster, establish which of the three they mean, because buying a wider connection does nothing for a user waiting on a round trip — and adding parallelism raises throughput while leaving each individual request exactly as slow as it was.

problem.name: The three speeds
problem.shape: Something is described as slow, and the word covers three different quantities with different remedies.
tell: a fix proposes a wider connection for a responsiveness problem
throughput targets are met and users complain
more workers were added and each request takes as long as before
a design adds a round trip to save bytes
problem.move: Name which quantity is failing before choosing a remedy. Spend bandwidth to buy latency — prefetch, batch, read ahead, replicate closer — and never the reverse. Raise throughput with parallelism, and expect it to leave individual latency untouched.
problem.invariant: Bandwidth improves far faster than latency, by more than the square as a rule of thumb, because bandwidth is an engineering purchase and latency is bounded by distance and the speed of light.
problem.breaks: Throughput and latency can move in opposite directions, and the technique that raises one often worsens the other. Batching improves throughput by making work wait, so a system tuned for the aggregate can degrade for every individual user while the dashboard improves.

cost.time: trading bandwidth for latency means transferring data nobody asked for, which is wasted when the guess is wrong
cost.space: prefetched and replicated data occupies memory and storage at every place you put it
cost.beats: minimising bytes transferred, which optimises the resource that is getting cheaper fastest

worked.problem: Does a faster connection make the system faster?
worked.reasoning:
It depends which of the three you mean, and for the complaint people usually have, a faster connection typically means a wider one — which does not help at all.

Separate them first. Latency is the delay before the first result. Bandwidth is how much can be in flight at once. Throughput is completed work per unit time. What is sold as a faster connection is almost always more bandwidth.

If the user is waiting for a round trip — a request goes out, a response comes back, and the payload is small — widening the pipe changes nothing. The time is dominated by distance and by the number of exchanges, and neither is affected by capacity. Doubling bandwidth halves the transfer time of a large payload and does approximately nothing to a small one.

If the user is waiting for a large transfer, then yes, bandwidth is exactly the constraint and more of it helps proportionally.

And if the system is failing to keep up with the volume of requests rather than being slow per request, that is throughput, which responds to parallelism — more workers, more replicas — while leaving each individual request as slow as it was. This is the case where a dashboard improves and users notice nothing.

The reason to reason this way rather than by instinct is that the three do not improve at the same rate, and that is structural. Across four technologies over two decades or more, bandwidth improved by factors between 120 and 2200 while latency improved only by factors between 4 and 20, with bandwidth improving by more than the square of latency's improvement as a rule of thumb. The causes are not incidental — transistor improvements help bandwidth more than latency, distance limits latency because the speed of light is fixed, and bandwidth is easier to sell. Or, as Clark put it, bandwidth problems can be cured with money and latency problems are harder because you cannot bribe God.

So the design instinct that follows is to spend bandwidth to buy latency and never the reverse: prefetch, batch, read ahead, send more than was asked for, and replicate data closer to where it is used. Moving a service physically nearer its callers is a latency intervention and is usually worth more than any amount of additional capacity.

The trap I would name is that batching improves throughput by making work wait. A system tuned for aggregate numbers can get worse for every individual user while the aggregate improves, which is why you need to know which quantity you are being asked to fix before you start.

problem.practice: Take a slow interaction in your system and decompose its time into waiting for round trips, transferring bytes, and queueing behind other work. Then say which of the three a wider connection would improve. Do the same for a proposal to add more workers.

beats.broke: Three different quantities get called speed, and a system can be excellent at one of them while being unusable because of another.
beats.fix: Separate them — the delay before the first result, the width of the pipe, and completed work per unit time — and identify which one the user actually experiences.
beats.cost: They are not independent and not equally improvable: the one users notice most has improved least and is bounded by physics rather than by engineering effort.
